title: Observed card spending continued to grow in August while households remained budget-conscious and the measurement system changed
source_unit: CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor powered by Affinity Solutions
geography: United States retail spending; anonymized permissioned credit and debit card transaction data

denominator.unit: more than 140 million credit and debit cards contributing to the Retail Monitor data; transaction and projection denominators are not individual households

total_retail_sales_mom.unit: percent seasonally adjusted month-over-month change in total retail sales excluding autos and gas

total_retail_sales_yoy.unit: percent seasonally adjusted year-over-year change in total retail sales excluding autos and gas

core_retail_sales_mom.unit: percent seasonally adjusted month-over-month change excluding autos, gas, and restaurants

core_retail_sales_yoy.unit: percent seasonally adjusted year-over-year change excluding autos, gas, and restaurants

consumer_mechanism.value: aggregate card spending remained positive while NRF described households as budget-conscious and using back-to-school promotions to stretch dollars; sales growth does not identify whether growth came from prices, quantities, affluent households, promotion, debt, or substitution

observations.method: CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor August 2026 release, powered by Affinity Solutions; the monitor uses anonymized card transactions, weights and projects the data to reflect U.S. consumers, and benchmarks to Census retail-sales totals.
observations.uncertainty: The public release does not provide household-level transaction records, income or demographic cross-tabs, category detail, quantities, margins, debt, or welfare measures. Card spending is not the same as household consumption capacity, affordability, or realized wellbeing.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers and retail transactions represented in the Affinity Solutions card-data frame; subgroup incidence and household concentration are not disclosed in this release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Positive sales can reflect inflation, promotions, essential purchases, credit use, or concentration among higher-capacity households rather than broad consumer resilience; flat or weak core growth can coexist with severe household pressure.

observations.period: September 2026 release; break in the retail measurement series

comparability_break.value: the new methodology weights and projects card data differently, so August month-over-month and year-over-year figures are not directly comparable with July's published figures

seasonal_adjustment.value: year-over-year comparisons are now seasonally adjusted, consistent with month-over-month figures

sector_detail.value: enhanced sector details and dollar levels are scheduled for the October full release

interpretation_rule.value: observed transaction growth should be read as a new-series August baseline until the revised history and sector detail permit a defensible time comparison

observations.method: NRF August report and Retail Monitor methodology note; this observation preserves the publisher's explicit warning against appending the new figures to the old monthly series.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not provide the full weighting model, merchant/category coverage, cardholder composition, or revised historical series; short-run changes cannot be decomposed into price, quantity, basket, or channel effects.
observations.subgroup: Researchers, policymakers, retailers, and analysts using high-frequency transaction data to infer U.S. consumer demand.
observations.counterinterpretation: A methodology break can improve representativeness and alignment with Census benchmarks; it may reduce apparent continuity but produce a stronger future series.

observations.period: 2026; high-frequency transaction infrastructure and consumer inference

denominator.unit: more than 150 million permissioned credit and debit cards linked to 95 million consumers in the Retail Monitor FAQ description

transaction_scale.value: nearly 86 billion annual transactions and more than 4 trillion US dollars in annual spending are described for the broader Affinity Solutions data platform

coverage.value: the monitor reports total retail sales, core retail sales, and nine distinct retail sectors plus restaurants, while deeper demographic and channel insights are restricted to members

privacy.value: Affinity states that the data are aggregated, grounded in consumer permission, and do not include personally identifiable information

next_test.value: join transaction growth to category, price, quantity, income, payment, debt, repeat purchase, and household-panel evidence before inferring value-seeking, resilience, or welfare

observations.method: NRF Retail Monitor FAQ describing data provenance, scale, calculation, privacy, and available outputs; platform-scale figures and August release estimates are kept as separate denominators.
observations.uncertainty: A large permissioned card frame can still differ from households by income, bank relationship, cash use, merchant coverage, geography, and card ownership; platform scale is not a public-use microdata release.
observations.subgroup: U.S. cardholders, retailers, analysts, and households whose spending is represented or omitted by the permissioned card-data frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: High-frequency transaction data can expose realized purchasing more quickly than surveys, but its commercial aggregation and benchmark choices can make household distribution and lived constraint less visible.

related_sources.claim: Census monthly retail-sales survey provides the official survey-based comparison and revision context.
BEA personal consumption expenditures provide a broader national-account measure of consumer spending.
Affinity Solutions describes its permissioned transaction-data platform and consumer-purchase insights.

boundary: This record adds an observed-consumption layer to the cultural and consumer atlas: anonymized permissioned card transactions show aggregate retail sales continuing to grow in August 2026 while households are described as budget-conscious. It does not establish household welfare, affordability, price versus quantity, subgroup distribution, debt, category substitution, repeat choice, or causal resilience; the August release also begins a new methodology series that is not directly comparable with July.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: NRF August 25, 2026 Retail Monitor press release, August report PDF, and FAQ were reviewed for transaction scale, August growth, methodology transition, benchmark, privacy, sector coverage, and interpretive limits.
